interest: This file offers valuable insights for interwar historians into the socioeconomic roots of Japan's political instability during the Great Depression. It clearly illustrates how technological gains and colonial agricultural development in Chosen and Taiwan boomeranged on metropolitan Japan by creating structural rice surpluses that drove prices below the cost of production, devastating the farming population already suffering from the collapse of the silk market. The documents highlight early experimentation with state-managed price corridors, government purchase programs, and production curtailments that closely paralleled Western depression-era interventions such as the U.S. Agricultural Adjustment Act. Furthermore, the file reveals how agrarian distress fed directly into domestic political turbulence—provoking parliamentary showdowns by the Seiyukai Party and calls for state monopolies—while intersecting with the monetary pressures of the gold standard and the Manchurian crisis.
overview: This State Department decimal file (894.61317, covering April 1930 to August 1934) documents Japan's struggle to manage a severe agrarian crisis caused by chronic rice overproduction and collapsing grain prices during the Great Depression. The file consists of Embassy Tokyo cross-reference sheets with attached report excerpts, a State Department Far Eastern Affairs memorandum, and an extensive Military Attaché intelligence report reproducing analyses from the Oriental Economist. These records trace the Japanese government's shift from decades of promoting rice production to enforcing production curtailment and market stabilization through successive revisions of the Rice Law and the Rice Control Law, which established official price ceilings and floors maintained by large-scale government purchases. The file also illuminates the domestic political repercussions of the surplus—including pressure from the opposition Seiyukai Party, calls for a state rice monopoly, and protests by impoverished farmers—as well as the imperial dimension of competition from Korean and Taiwanese rice imports and the concurrent financial debates over reimposing the gold embargo during the 1931 Manchurian crisis.

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet and attached extract from Embassy Tokyo Report No. 42 regarding the collapse of rice prices and recommendations of the Rice Investigation Commission.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet indexes Despatch No. 91 (Report No. 42) from Ambassador William R. Castle, Jr., transmitting an extract on the price of rice under the government's retrenchment policy. Following a steep decline in rice prices, the Rice Investigation Commission drafted a plan on March 20, 1930, to supplement the existing Rice Law. The commission recommended fixing statutory maximum and minimum standard prices, providing low-interest credit to agricultural product warehouses, regulating Korean rice shipments from the Government-General of Chosen to Japan Proper, and establishing state supervision over exports and imports.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Despatch No. 91 with Report Extract on Rice Prices and Proposed Legislation

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet summarizing Embassy Tokyo Despatch No. 38 regarding a sharp decline in rice prices following a bumper crop forecast and related government financial challenges.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet indexes Despatch No. 38 from Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes concerning the severe economic distress caused by an anticipated 12 percent increase in the 1930 rice harvest over 1929. The projected excess caused prices to plunge from 29-30 yen per koku in early September to around 17 yen in October, severely harming farmers already suffering from silk industry losses. The note adds that the government's major preoccupations during the month included preparing the draft budget for the Diet, paring down Navy budget demands, stabilizing rice prices, and tackling unemployment.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Despatch No. 38 on Rice Price Decline and Budgetary Problems

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet and attached extract from Embassy Tokyo Report No. 74 regarding unprecedented rice yields and government plans to purchase surplus grain.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet indexes Report No. 74 from Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes concerning an unprecedentedly large rice crop, with supply expected to exceed demand by 9,571,000 koku. Although per capita consumption was officially estimated at 1.114 koku, embassy observers viewed that figure as excessive compared to the actual rate of 1.086 koku. To regulate supply and halt further price declines that threatened agricultural distress, the Rice Committee submitted a plan for the government to purchase 2,000,000 koku of rice during December.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Report No. 74 with Extract on Rice Crop Estimates and Government Purchasing Plans

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet and attached extract from Embassy Tokyo Report No. 131 on official rice harvest statistics and inadequate state funds for price stabilization.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet indexes Report No. 131 from Chargé d'Affaires Eugene H. Dooman forwarding official harvest figures announced by the Department of Agriculture and Forestry. The actual 1930 crop reached 66,853,000 koku, an increase of 12.3 percent over 1929 and 12.5 percent over the five-year average. Agricultural societies across Japan actively lobbied the government to purchase large quantities of grain to bolster prices, but the remaining balance of 40,000,000 yen allocated for rice price regulation was considered insufficient for effective intervention.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Report No. 131 with Extract on Final Rice Crop Figures and Price Regulation Funds

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet and attached report extract concerning public and political agitation in Japan to reimpose the gold export embargo amid the Manchurian crisis.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet indexes Report No. 404 from Chargé d'Affaires Edwin L. Neville regarding intense public pressure in November 1931 to reimpose an embargo on gold specie exports. Opposition party Diet members, newspapers like the Tokyo Jiji, business leaders in the Tokyo Chamber of Commerce, and a best-selling book by Sanji Muto all clamored for an immediate ban on gold exports. Depleted gold reserves of 542,716,000 yen, military expenses in Manchuria, Chinese boycotts, and the depreciation of sterling exacerbated financial strains, although the Finance Minister reiterated in an Osaka speech his refusal to abandon free gold exports.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Report No. 404 with Extract on Agitation for Reimposition of the Gold Embargo

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet and attached extract from Embassy Tokyo Despatch No. 541 regarding the Ministry of Agriculture's reversal from encouraging rice output to curtailing production.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet indexes Despatch No. 541 from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reporting the Minister of Agriculture's September 7, 1933 decision to reverse longstanding production-boosting policies due to chronic surpluses and falling prices. The government decided to discontinue subsidies for land reclamation, irrigation projects, and farm readjustments. Production control measures were extended across the empire to Chosen and Taiwan, and as an initial stabilization measure, the government arranged to purchase 350,000 koku of the new crop starting October 1 to prevent distressed market dumping.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Despatch No. 541 with Extract on Policy Reversal toward Rice Production Curtailment

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet and attached extract from Embassy Tokyo Report No. 823 regarding political conflict over the rice crisis and proposals for a government monopoly.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet indexes Report No. 823 from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew detailing political controversy surrounding a 17-million-koku rice surplus and severe agrarian impoverishment. The opposition Seiyukai Party under Dr. Kisaburo Suzuki demanded an extraordinary Diet session to enact new control legislation, threatening to force the government's resignation if it refused. Press commentary was divided, with the Asahi urging a state monopoly while the Japan Times stressed that a monopoly would not absorb the massive surplus or relieve farmer poverty; furthermore, high production costs made exporting surplus rice impossible despite yen depreciation.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Report No. 823 with Extract on Political Demands for Rice Control Legislation

subfiles.about: Memorandum by Far Eastern Affairs officer circulating Tokyo Military Attaché Report No. 7372 on Japanese rice price stabilization.
subfiles.summary: This Department of State Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum circulates a report from the Tokyo Military Attaché on Japan's rice problem for the information of department officers. The memo outlines how Japan's 1919 Rice Law established a price-index mechanism under which the government purchased rice when prices dipped below fixed levels and sold rice when prices rose. The author highlights the report's conclusion that this interventionist mechanism successfully kept rice quotations within legally defined parameters.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum Circulating Military Attaché Report on Japanese Rice Regulation

subfiles.about: Intelligence report transmitting an analytical article and commentary from the Oriental Economist on historical rice trade, price control legislation, and systemic overproduction in Japan.
subfiles.from: T. M. Martin and William C. Crane
subfiles.summary: This intelligence report by Assistant Military Attaché Captain T. M. Martin, approved by Military Attaché Major William C. Crane, provides an in-depth historical analysis of Japan's rice economy from 1865 to 1934 based on an article and editorial in the Oriental Economist. It traces Japan's evolution from a rice-exporting nation before 1895 into a structural importer, followed by self-sufficiency and severe overproduction after 1930 driven by soaring domestic and colonial yields in Chosen and Taiwan. The report details the mechanics of the 1921 Rice Control Law and its 1931 revision, which established a cost-of-production floor price of 163.10 yen per ton and a ceiling of 213.50 yen per ton, enforced by government purchases totaling 2.1 million tons. While state intervention succeeded in holding market prices around 172 yen per ton, the report warns that annual surpluses of 10,000,000 koku would eventually exhaust state financial resources, likely forcing the creation of a full government rice monopoly.
subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report No. 7372 on 'The Rice Problem' in Japan
